Kuwait Petroleum Corp Files for Insolvency, Operations Disrupted as Crisis Unfolds

KUWAIT CITY, June 17 — State-backed oil giant Kuwait Petroleum Corp has filed for insolvency, throwing the country’s energy sector into turmoil and raising urgent questions about the future of its vast operations, company officials confirmed Monday.

The move comes after weeks of mounting financial pressure and failed restructuring efforts, with the company now formally entering court-supervised administration. The insolvency filing, which a KPC spokesperson described as “a last resort,” has already led to the suspension of some refining and export activities, according to multiple sources familiar with operations.

“Kuwait Petroleum Corp has taken this difficult decision to protect the interests of its stakeholders,” the company said in a statement. “We are working closely with our advisors and relevant authorities to stabilize our operations and minimize disruption.”

The announcement marks an unprecedented event for the Middle East’s energy sector. KPC is one of the region’s largest oil producers, responsible for a significant share of Kuwait’s national revenue. The company employs over 15,000 people and operates refineries, export terminals, and a vast pipeline network.

As of midday Monday, several key facilities, including the Shuaiba and Sabriya refineries, were operating at reduced capacity, while contracts with some international buyers had been temporarily suspended. A senior KPC manager, speaking on condition of anonymity, said, “We are doing everything we can to maintain critical exports, but the insolvency process is having a direct impact on day-to-day operations.”

Trade unions representing KPC workers expressed concern about job security and unpaid wages. “Our members have not received full salaries for the past month,” said Nasser Al-Mutairi, head of the Kuwait Oil Workers’ Union. “Many employees are worried about their future and the future of the country’s oil sector.”

Analysts say the insolvency could have far-reaching consequences for Kuwait’s economy, which relies heavily on oil revenues. “This is a seismic event for Kuwait and the region,” said Dr. Laila Hassan, an energy analyst at Gulf Resources Consultancy. “The immediate concern is operational continuity, but the longer-term implications for investment and energy security are profound.”

A government official, declining to be named, said talks were ongoing with creditors and potential restructuring partners, including the local banks Al-Sabah Capital and Gulf Investors Group. “We are considering all options,” the official said.

As the administration process unfolds, market participants and international partners are watching closely, with further operational disruptions likely in the coming days. The government has yet to announce a rescue package or further policy measures.
